faq: What makes a good pilot task?
Something repeated often, with clear right and wrong answers and low risk if it goes wrong, such as sorting mail or drafting product notes. We help you choose in the first call.
Will the pilot become the final system?
Sometimes it can be kept and extended, other times it is a test to throw away. We tell you which, and what a full version would involve, before you decide.
Who pays for the tools used in the pilot?
Any subscription or usage fee is billed to you by the tool maker, and we keep it as small as possible by using free or low cost plans while testing.
What if the pilot shows it does not work?
That is a useful result and still counts as delivered. You learn it cheaply, and we explain the reasons and what else you could try instead.

desc:
An AI pilot project with real results tests one idea on a small scale before you build the whole thing. Ecom Swift LLC sets up a working version in your own accounts, runs it on real examples and tells you whether to scale, change or stop.

## What is an AI pilot project?

An AI pilot project is a small, time-limited test of one task, built to answer a single question: does this work for our business? It uses your real examples, such as actual emails, orders or documents, and measures the outcome against a goal agreed in advance.

A pilot is not a demo. A demo shows what a tool can do on a perfect example. A pilot shows what it does on your messy, ordinary work.

## Why test before you build

Full builds cost real money and real attention. If the idea turns out to be a poor fit, you learn that after the spend. Typical surprises include answers that are close but not good enough to send, tasks that look repetitive but hide many exceptions, and staff who find the tool slower than doing the job by hand.

A pilot brings those surprises forward, when changing course is cheap. It also gives you something a sales page cannot: evidence from your own data, in your own tools, with your own people.

## How a pilot improves your decision

A pilot turns an opinion into a measurement. Before we start, we agree what success looks like, for example time per task, how many outputs were usable without edits, or how often a person had to step in. After the test, we compare the result with that measure.

This works because the test uses real examples. Accuracy shows up in the first batch. Time saved shows up when someone from your team uses the pilot for an actual shift. The final summary then supports one of three clear choices: scale it up, adjust it and test again, or stop. Results from a small test cannot predict every future outcome, so we state what the test did and did not cover.

## What a good pilot includes

- One clearly defined task, small enough to finish and common enough to matter.
- A success measure agreed before any work starts.
- A working setup in your own accounts and tools.
- A set of real examples, run through the pilot and recorded.
- A record of what needed fixing, and why.
- A trial with real staff members, in the larger packages.
- Before and after timing where the task allows it.
- A short results summary with a plain recommendation.
- A plan and quote to scale up, where the result supports it.

## How we run the pilot

First we choose the task together. We look for something repetitive, with clear inputs and outputs, and low risk if a result is wrong. Then we agree the success measure and collect the real examples you will test with.

We build the small version in tools you own, so nothing is locked inside our accounts. We run the examples, log each result and note every correction. The Basic package covers one task and a short results note. Standard adds an agreed success measure, more examples and a trial with two staff members. Premium can cover two tasks, measure the time before and after, involve a larger group of staff and close with a plan and quote to scale. Add-ons include extra test examples, a staff feedback survey and a full build quote.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Pick a task that happens often and has a clear right answer.
- Agree on the success measure before the test begins.
- Use real examples, including the awkward ones.
- Let staff try the pilot and give honest feedback.
- Be ready to stop if the evidence says so.

**Avoid:**
- Choosing a task that is rare, urgent or high risk.
- Judging the pilot by a few good examples only.
- Changing the success measure after you see the results.
- Using sensitive customer details when sample versions would do.
- Assuming a pilot is automatically the final system.

## Who this is for

A pilot suits an owner who has a promising idea but does not want to commit to a full build. It suits a team lead who must justify spending to a manager and needs numbers. It also suits a business that tried a tool once, had mixed results and wants a fair, structured retest.

Tools used in a pilot are paid for directly by you, in your own accounts, where a paid plan is needed. Our price covers the work.

## What we need from you

Tell us the task, why it matters and who does it today. Send a set of real examples, with private details removed where possible. Nominate the staff members who will try the pilot. We never ask for passwords. Where we need to work inside a tool, you add us as a staff, team or developer user with only the access the pilot needs.
